claims.text: The dominant mechanism governing wear performance in high-entropy-alloy protective coatings is formation of a protective tribofilm during sliding.
Sliding can produce a stable oxide or spinel film on the coating surface.
The tribofilm minimizes direct metal-to-metal or asperity contact.
Suppressing direct contact through the tribofilm lowers the coating wear rate.
Suppressing direct contact through the tribofilm lowers the friction coefficient.
Increasing oxygen partial pressure promotes rapid formation and stabilization of a protective tribofilm.
A durable tribofilm prevents severe abrasive wear.
A durable tribofilm prevents severe adhesive wear.
Oxidation becomes significant at elevated temperatures of approximately 500 to 900 °C.
At high oxygen partial pressure, especially at elevated temperature, the coating will develop a continuous tribofilm.
High-oxygen testing will yield lower wear rates than an inert or low-oxygen baseline.
High-oxygen testing will yield lower friction coefficients than an inert or low-oxygen baseline.
In nitrogen or argon, oxygen is insufficient to initiate protective tribofilm formation.
The protective oxygen effect should hold from approximately 500 to 900 °C.
Alloy composition, microstructure, and processing conditions may change the nature and protective quality of the tribofilm and shift the applicable temperature range.
Oxidation of a high-entropy alloy can produce a non-protective oxide scale.
Lack of oxide coherence or continuity can make the resulting scale non-protective.
Failure of increased oxygen pressure to produce a continuous protective film or improve both wear and friction relative to the inert control would falsify the hypothesis.
